opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's really the heart of what we were trying to understand with MrT5. The basic idea is that byte-level models like ByT5 are wonderful in a lot of ways. They're tokenizer-free, robust to spelling variation and noise, and they handle many languages more equitably. But they're expensive, because byte sequences are so much longer than subword sequences. So we asked: can the model learn to shorten its own sequence as it goes?

The key design choice is a learned deletion gate placed after a small number of early encoder layers. That placement matters because of what those early layers are doing. In the first few layers, attention lets each byte position gather information from its neighbors. By the time you reach the gate, a position no longer represents just one raw byte. It carries some contextualized information about the characters around it, and in some sense about the word or morpheme it belongs to.

That's what makes deletion safe. When the gate drops a token, we aren't throwing that information away. It has already been absorbed, or merged, into the tokens that remain. So I like to say that "deletion" is really implicit merging. The early attention layers do the merging, and the gate just decides which positions are now redundant.

Placement involves a trade-off. If you delete too early, say right at the input, there's been no time for that information to spread, and you lose content. If you delete too late, you've already paid most of the compute cost of the long sequence. We found that a few layers in is a nice sweet spot. You get enough contextualization to preserve performance, and you still save a lot of compute in the remaining layers and in the decoder's cross-attention.

What's really cool is what the model learns to delete. Without being told anything about linguistic structure, it tends to keep positions around word boundaries and drop many of the positions in the middle of words. That suggests it's discovering something like a soft, contextual tokenization on its own. And because the decision is dynamic, it adapts to the input. Different languages and different scripts get compressed at different rates, which a fixed tokenizer just can't do.

So to me, the early attention layers are what turn a crude idea like "just delete some bytes" into something principled. They build the representations that make compression possible in the first place.

r001.rationale: It says early attention lets each byte position gather information from neighbors and explicitly describes those layers as doing the merging.

r002.rationale: It explains that when the gate drops a token, its information has already been absorbed or merged into the tokens that remain.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really at the heart of how MrT5 works. The core idea is that we take ByT5, which operates directly on bytes, and we insert a learned deletion gate after one of the early encoder layers, say layer three. That gate decides which byte positions get dropped before the rest of the encoder sees them. And the question you're asking is, why does that work at all? Why is it okay to throw away positions so early?

The answer is that those first few layers of attention are doing a lot of work to contextualize the bytes. By the time you get to layer three, each position isn't really representing just one byte anymore. It's a mixture of information from its neighbors. So when the gate deletes, say, the second, third, and fourth bytes of a word, that information isn't gone. It has already been attended to and folded into the representations of the surrounding positions that survive.

What we actually see when we look at the deletion patterns is really interesting. The model tends to keep the first byte or so of a word and delete the rest, and often it preserves spaces or boundary characters. So it's learning something that looks a bit like an implicit tokenization. But it's dynamic, it's conditioned on the context, and it's not a fixed vocabulary. It varies by language, which was one of the motivations, because standard subword tokenizers are really inequitable across languages. Some languages get many more tokens per sentence than others.

And this depends on attention being in place before the gate. If you put the gate at layer zero, before any attention, you'd just be deleting raw byte embeddings with no context, and the model has no way to compress information into the kept positions. We did experiment with where to place the gate, and you need a few layers of attention for the merging to be meaningful. But you also don't want it too late, because then you've already paid most of the compute cost of the full-length sequence, and the whole point is efficiency.

So I think of early attention as doing the actual merging. The gate is just deciding where the merge boundaries are. The attention has done the work of pooling the bytes into the representations that remain.

r001.rationale: It says early attention contextualizes each byte by mixing in information from neighboring positions, and describes that as the actual merging.

r002.rationale: It explains that a byte can be deleted after attention has folded its information into representations at positions that survive.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that the early layers give you a signal about which tokens could be grouped together. Attention is contextual, so it can reveal relationships that you wouldn’t necessarily capture with a fixed rule, like always merging adjacent tokens in pairs.

With dynamic token merging, you use that signal to decide where to keep fine-grained representations and where you can compress the sequence. The later layers then operate on fewer representations, which can reduce computation.

The tradeoff is that early-layer attention is still an imperfect signal. Two tokens attending to each other doesn’t necessarily mean they’re interchangeable. So the important question is whether it gives you enough information to merge selectively without losing distinctions that later layers need.

r001.rationale: The response describes early-layer attention as a signal for deciding which tokens to group, but does not say attention already combines information from other tokens into each token as a form of merging.

r002.rationale: The response mentions selectively compressing the sequence, but does not explain that a token may be dropped after its information has been incorporated into other tokens through early-layer attention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of early-layer attention as a signal for deciding which tokens can be combined. Before you’ve done much processing, it’s hard to tell whether two tokens are redundant in context. Those first attention layers let tokens exchange information, so their representations start to reflect how they’re being used, rather than just their identities.

That gives you a basis for making a dynamic decision: which tokens appear to carry similar information in this particular input, and which need to stay separate? If you can merge some of that redundancy early, the later layers operate on a shorter sequence, which is where the computational savings come from.

The tradeoff is that early representations are still developing. Looking similar at an early layer doesn’t necessarily mean two tokens are interchangeable. So the key is finding a point where you have enough contextual information to make useful merging decisions, but you’re still early enough to save substantial computation.

r001.rationale: It says early attention layers let tokens exchange information so each token’s representation reflects contextual use, which conveys attention combining information across tokens.

r002.rationale: It discusses merging redundant tokens based on contextual similarity, but does not say a token may be dropped because its information has already been incorporated into other tokens through attention.
